column3: Near-verbatim parallel: hardship seizes communities so that they may humble themselves, whereas the focus records their failure to do so.
Its removal of punishment followed by covenant-breaking reinforces the surrounding pattern of relief that does not produce a lasting return.
It joins standing before the Lord with tasting punishment, but it does not address punishment's intended call to humble return.
It explicitly says that punishment was inflicted so that the people might return, supplying the positive purpose absent in the focus.
The next ayah continues the same punitive sequence, escalating from the unresponsive punishment of the focus to severe despair.
It presents the punishment of the Lord as the consequence of disobedience, supporting the focus's Lord-directed punitive frame.
Its denial that steadfast believers became weak or yielded under suffering uses the same yielding language in a contrasting faithful setting.
The immediately preceding ayah explains the people's persistence: even mercy and lifted harm would leave them wandering in rebellion.
It confirms that divine punishment is painful but adds no connection to humility, supplication, or response to affliction.
Within the surah, punishment makes the affluent cry out; this sharpens the focus's point that their later punishment still produces no humble pleading.
Affliction prompts a plea and promise of belief, then relief; it closely contrasts the focus's refusal even to humble themselves.
The food called dari' does not clarify the focus's punishment, failure to yield, or appeal to the Lord.
Following the destructive blast, they cannot rise or defend themselves, depicting the disabling consequence of divine punishment.
Reverent fear of the Lord provides a limited positive contrast to the focus's lack of responsive humility.
It portrays a people seized after rejecting all signs, a related but less specific instance of punitive taking.
Responding to the Lord supplies the positive counterpart to the focus's refusal to yield to their Lord under punishment.
Job calls upon his Lord when harm touches him, directly contrasting a suffering person's responsive appeal with the focus's non-supplication.
The command to seize a condemned person depicts punishment but has no meaningful link to humble return or supplication.
The inability to scale or breach the barrier is unrelated to punishment producing no humility.
The arrogance of Pharaoh's chiefs identifies the proud resistance that helps explain the focus's refusal to yield within the surah's history.
The mention of mercy from the Lord does not clarify the focus's punishment or unresponsive behavior.
Those who demand the punishment's arrival are warned that it will come suddenly, supporting the focus's punitive setting without its response motif.
God removes Job's harm after his appeal, providing the responsive and merciful counterpart to the focus's affliction without supplication.
Praise of the Lord in Paradise does not clarify refusal to humble oneself under punishment.
The statement that heaven and earth did not weep for them adds no connection to the focus's response to punishment.
The promised regret is a nearby consequence of the same surah's rejected warning and helps frame the focus's hardened response.
Calling God Lord of Sirius does not clarify punishment, humility, or supplication.
Night worship before the Lord is a broad positive contrast to the focus's refusal to humble themselves before their Lord.
After the plague is lifted, the people break their promise; it continues the affliction-relief-return pattern that contextualizes the focus.
It commands disbelievers to taste punishment but does not connect that punishment with humility or return.
Near-verbatim parallel: communities are seized with adversity and distress so that they may humble themselves.
Resurrection does not clarify the focus's immediate punishment or failure to supplicate.
Forgiveness and honor from the Lord do not illuminate the focus's punitive non-response.
After ignored reminders and deceptive abundance, sudden seizure leaves the people despairing, a close pattern of hardened response to divine correction.
It states that no rival can remove harm or withhold mercy, grounding the focus's implication that humble appeal should be directed to the Lord alone.
Receiving what the Lord gives the righteous does not clarify punishment or the refusal to yield.
Those asking for punishment are already enclosed by Hell, intensifying the focus's warning that punishment is not a route they control.
This nearby accusation of fabrication shows the denial underlying the surah's later refusal to respond to punishment.
The afflicted explicitly ask their Lord to remove the punishment, directly contrasting the focus's statement that its people do not plead.
It answers those who hasten punishment by affirming God's unfailing promise, related to the focus's punitive warning but not its response.
The temporary lifting of punishment followed by relapse closely parallels the surrounding cycle of affliction, relief, and persistent refusal.
Steadfast confession that God is our Lord is a broad positive counterpart to refusing to yield to one's Lord.
Reverent fear of the Lord offers a limited contrast to the focus's lack of humbled response.
The loss and abiding punishment of those with light scales supplies a later surah outcome for the resistant people.
Fear of the punishment of their Lord is the responsive disposition missing from the focus's punished people.
It contrasts those who answer their Lord with those who do not, assigning the latter terrible reckoning and Hell.
Moses calls upon his Lord against a criminal people, another Lord-directed appeal within an affliction-and-punishment setting.
The repeated challenge about the Lord's favors does not clarify the focus's punishment or absence of supplication.
Its account of repeated rejection after clear signs helps explain hardened unbelief but lacks the focus's affliction-and-humility pattern.
The same surah depicts arrogant nighttime rejection, a proximate expression of the resistance exposed in the focus.
Turning away from the Lord's remembrance leads into an ever-rising punishment, explicitly linking refusal of the Lord to punitive consequence.
Its future judgment of disagreement does not clarify punishment intended to elicit humility.
The command to worship God and avoid corruption is only a general antecedent to the punishment in the focus.
Worship of the Lord is a broad positive counterpart to refusing to humble oneself before Him.
It explicitly commands calling upon the Lord with humble supplication, directly supplying the action denied in the focus.
This nearby dismissal of the messenger as mad contributes to the surah's pattern of refusal that precedes the focus's punishment.
The identification of the Lord of Moses and Aaron does not clarify punishment or humble response.
The greeting and meal offered to Abraham are unrelated to the focus's punitive setting.
After denial and arrogance, the earthquake seizes the people and leaves them prone in their homes, a concrete punitive parallel.
Magnifying the Lord is a general positive contrast to withholding humbled response under punishment.
It explicitly joins remembrance of the Lord with humble, fearful, quiet supplication, the response absent in the focus.
Humble attentiveness in prayer is a surah-internal positive counterpart to the focus's failure to yield to the Lord.
The Lord's full knowledge on that day supports accountability but does not connect punishment to humble pleading.
Persistent doubt after clear proofs illustrates hardening, but it lacks the focus's punishment and supplication language.
It identifies God alone as remover of harm, supporting why affliction should lead the focus's people to their Lord.
Trust in the Lord's guidance is a broad positive response to danger, only loosely related to humble pleading under punishment.
The failed exchange of guidance for error does not clarify punishment or response to it.
The successful people with heavy scales form the immediate surah contrast to the punished losers of 23:103.
Rescue from painful punishment is relevant, but the verse does not address its purpose in eliciting humility.
They dispute warnings of divine assault, showing resistance to the warning that precedes punitive seizure.
The divine names Merciful and Compassionate do not clarify the focus's failure to humble themselves under punishment.
It compares a worldly punishment with the greater punishment of the Hereafter, supporting the focus's warning frame without its response motif.
Near-verbatim parallel: Pharaoh's people are seized with years of scarcity and loss of crops so that they may remember.
Mocking believers makes the rejecters forget God's remembrance, a surah-internal mechanism for the focus's unresponsive condition.
Fear of the Lord before the Hour is a broad admonition, not a parallel to punishment failing to produce supplication.
Rebellion against the Lord's command is followed by seizure through the thunderbolt, a direct punitive pattern.
Pharaoh's claim about expulsion from the land does not clarify the focus's punishment or humility.
It commands the guilty to taste enduring punishment because they forgot the meeting of their day, a related account of retributive consequence.
Arrogance after clear signs and inability to escape describe resistant wrongdoers but not their response to punishment.
The surah closes with a plea for forgiveness and mercy to the Lord, a positive counterpart to the focus's refusal to plead.
Wrongdoers are told to taste enduring punishment as recompense for their earnings, supporting the focus's retributive setting.
The disbeliever's stance against his Lord broadly matches resistance, but it lacks affliction or humble pleading.
The Lord's creative knowledge does not clarify the focus's punishment or refusal to supplicate.
Lack of protectors and a path after divine misguidance does not clarify the focus's stated response to punishment.
It juxtaposes entry into mercy with painful punishment for wrongdoers, but does not address humbled return.
Destruction of earlier counterparts serves as a warning of punishment for persistent denial.
The prayer that the Lord establish prayer and accept supplication is a general positive contrast to the focus's non-supplication.
The abode of peace with the Lord does not clarify punishment or a failure to respond to it.
It names the worst punishment and ultimate loss, extending the focus's warning toward its final consequence.
Earlier generations are destroyed after injustice and rejection of clear messengers, a general punitive precedent.
The question to the messengers about their mission does not clarify the focus's affliction or response.
The repeated challenge about the Lord's favors does not clarify punishment or humble supplication.
Repeated burning so that they taste punishment gives a vivid instance of retribution, without the focus's intended return.
Choosing punishment over forgiveness culminates in endurance of the Fire, a related image of deliberate attachment to punitive consequence.
David's favor and softened iron are unrelated to punishment failing to produce humility.
It explicitly contrasts gratitude with severe divine punishment for ingratitude, clarifying punishment as a response to rejected divine care.
The Lord's irreversible command and unavoidable punishment portray a punishment that can no longer be turned back.
God's acceptance of repentance supplies a distant positive counterpart to the focus's refusal to turn back and plead.
Universal glorification of God does not clarify the focus's punishment or human non-response.
Human ingratitude toward his Lord names the underlying refusal of the sustaining Lord that the focus exposes under punishment.
It asks whom people would invoke if God's punishment or the Hour came, directly framing calamity as a test of exclusive appeal to God.
It states that people would call upon God alone under punishment and that He may remove the harm, the positive response denied in the focus.
Exact corrective parallel: when God's punishment came, they did not humble themselves, because their hearts had hardened.
After hardship is exchanged for ease, the people dismiss prior affliction and are seized suddenly, extending the pattern of unlearned correction.
God tests the people with good and bad conditions so that they may return, explicitly giving adversity a corrective purpose.
Despite recurrent yearly testing, they neither repent nor remember, closely paralleling the focus's failure to respond to corrective affliction.
When harm touches a person, he calls upon God in every posture; once harm is removed, he passes on, a direct affliction-and-response parallel.
In a sea storm, people call sincerely upon God and then transgress after rescue, closely matching the wider distress-relief-relapse cycle.
It states that when harm touches people, they cry out to God, directly contrasting the focus's absence of supplication.
After God removes harm, a group associates others with Him, supplying the relief followed by relapse pattern.
A secure community that denied God's favors is made to taste hunger and fear, a concrete punitive deprivation for ingratitude.
When harm befalls people at sea, those invoked besides God disappear and they call upon Him, directly linking distress to exclusive appeal.
When people sense divine might, they flee, a contrasting reaction to punishment that still belongs to the same judgment scene.
The immediately prior command not to cry out because no help will come clarifies the futile cries that contrast with 23:76's lack of humble pleading.
The prophet asks why his people hasten evil before good and why they do not seek forgiveness so that they may receive mercy.
In danger at sea, people call upon God with sincere devotion, then associate others after rescue, directly paralleling distress and failed return.
When harm touches people, they call upon their Lord turning to Him; after mercy, some associate others, a close positive-and-relapse counterpart.
Overwhelming waves prompt sincere prayer to God, but post-rescue responses divide, making it a direct distress-and-supplication parallel.
The nearer punishment is explicitly given so that people may return, directly stating the corrective aim implicated in the focus.
When harm touches a person, he calls upon his Lord turning to Him; after favor, he forgets the appeal, closely matching the response cycle.
When harm touches man, he calls upon God, but after a favor he treats it as self-earned, again joining distress, appeal, and relapse.
On seeing God's might, people finally profess belief, showing a belated response to punishment rather than the focus's hardened non-response.
Faith after seeing God's might no longer benefits them, defining the limit beyond which a response to punishment is too late.
When evil touches man, he becomes a person of expansive supplication, a direct contrast to the focus's refusal to plead.
